evidence_occurrences.evidence_text:
We prioritized Int8 weight-only (W8A16) and FP8 quantization, which delivered faster inference than BF16 with minimal accuracy loss. The reduced weight size also freed up memory for larger key-value caches.

[ReDrafter](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-tensorrt-llm-now-supports-recurrent-drafting-for-optimizing-llm-inference/) is a speculative decoding technique developed by Apple, and implemented in TensorRT-LLM. We trained a ReDrafter head on a random subset of problems from OpenMathReasoning-1 dataset. Using these problems we generated 100k solutions with the target model. The resulting redrafter generated 3 tokens for every LLM step with 65% acceptance rate delivering a speed up of approximately 1.8X. The TensorRT-LLM repo’s example implementation has an example for a non quantised llama, so we needed some changes to make it work. We tried other drafting methods, but could not get them to work as well. Especially LLM drafting should work and may be better.

evidence_occurrences.evidence_text:
We developed a method for integrating code execution into long reasoning generations. Our initial attempts to elicit Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) generations from DeepSeek-R1 through simple prompting proved unsuccessful. We hypothesize that these models struggle to deviate from their standard solution format due to extensive training on reasoning tasks and limited exposure to instruction-following. To overcome this challenge, we built a pipeline that starts with a small-scale reasoning finetuning of an instruction-following model, [LIMO](https://huggingface.co/GAIR/LIMO). By prompting this model to generate long-reasoning TIR solutions followed by aggressive quality filtering, we established an initial dataset suitable for training. Through multiple iterations of training, generation, and filtering, we constructed a 1.7M TIR solution set that was crucial for improving the accuracy of our final models.

For final stage TIR training, the 1.7M solutions are aggressively filtered down to 15K samples based on number of code executions and correctness of answers.

evidence_occurrences.evidence_text:
We observed a dramatic performance boost when we used pretrained foreign language monolingual Transformer models from HuggingFace for the test-set languages(e.g., Camembert for french samples, Rubert for russian, BerTurk for turkish, BETO for spanish etc.).

We finetuned models for each of the 6 languages - by combining translations of the 2018 Toxic Comments together with pseudo-labels for samples in that specific language (initially from the XLM-R multilingual models), training the corresponding monolingual model, predicting the same samples then blending it back with the “main branch” of all predictions. It was synergistic in that training model A -> training model B -> training model A etc. lead to continual performance improvements.

For each model run, we’d reload weight initalizations from the pretrained models to prevent overfitting. In other words, the continuing improvements we saw were being driven by refinements in the pseudo-labels we were providing to the models as training data.

For a given monolingual model, predicting only test-set samples in that language worked best. Translating test-set samples in other languages to the model's language and predicting them worsened performance.

### Finetuning pre-trained foreign language monolingual FastText models

After we exhausted the HuggingFace monolingual model library, we trained monolingual FastText Bidirectional GRU models a la 2018 Toxic Comments, using pretrained embeddings for the test-set languages, to continue refining the test set predictions (albeit with a lower weight when combined with the main branch of predictions) and saw a small but meaningful performance boost (0.9536 to 0.9544).

1.   **Chemistry-specific foundation models aren't very good:** In one round of experiments without pseudolabeled training data, the best CV wMAE score achieved with `ChemBERTa` was 0.0634, the best score achieved with `polyBERT` was 0.592, and the best score achieved with `ModernBERT-base` was 0.0584. So, the general-purpose model beat anything chemistry or polymer specific.
2.   **Bigger models aren't better:** Using tuning and testing methodology identical to #1, above, `ModernBERT-large` scored 0.0587 whereas `-base` scored 0.0584. So scaling up made the score worse. `DeBERTa-v3-large`'s scores also sucked, so I don't think this behavior was isolated to the ModernBERT family.

While thinking about why that might be, I recalled that the ModernBERT family also scores disproportionately well on programming-related benchmarks, and had a relatively large amount of code in its pretraining dataset, so this caused me to wonder if a model trained on an even higher ratio of code to natural language would score even better, which led me to trying `CodeBERT`. `CodeBERT` wound up being ~tied for being my best single model. Slightly better than `ModernBERT-base` in cross-validation testing and on the public leaderboard, slightly worse on the private leaderboard, but generally close enough to be within margin of error, and substantially better than anything purely trained on chemistry or English data.
